rows.name: 1-2 World 1-2 underground area (layout data and enemy data)
rows.notes: World 1-2 (underground). Reach deterministically: reset_emulator, pause immediately, step_frame 60 (title), then write CPU $075F=0 (world 1), $075C=1 (HUD level digit 2), $0760=2 (area index), step 2, play_input [{start,6},{},200]. Live at level start: $074E=2 (underground area type), $074F=0, $0750=$C0 (area header), game_mode $0770=1, TIME 400. LAYOUT: the level loader (CPU $9C22) resolves the area's layout pointer through low table $9D2C / high $9D4E with base $9D28[$074E=2]; live $E7/$E8 = $AC37. $AC37 is the first 2-byte object record; the 2-byte area header sits at $AC35 = 48 0F. Object records are [type,x] pairs (parser at CPU $9514 does LDA ($E7),Y / CMP #$FD). The record stream ends with the $FD terminator at $ACD7; the next area's header starts at $ACD8. So the whole 1-2 layout datum is prgRom 0x2C35..0x2CD7, 163 bytes (header 0x2C35..0x2C36, object records 0x2C37..0x2CD6, $FD at 0x2CD7). ENEMY DATA: the loader resolves it through base $9CE0 + low $9CE4 / high $9D06; live $E9/$EA = $A0D8. The enemy list runs from $A0D8 to its first $FF end-marker at $A104. So the 1-2 enemy datum is prgRom 0x20D8..0x2104, 45 bytes. PROOFS (both ledgered one-byte prgRom writes, then reset_emulator + re-reach, then undone with undo_edit): (1) layout - write prgRom 0x2C3C (the x byte of the first real object, type $A7 at x=0) 0x00 -> 0x1F: the first screen loaded rearranged (the start-area ground/terrace object was moved away, Mario left in mid-air, later objects pulled into the first screen), while RAM still read $074E=2 and the timer 398, proving 0x2C3C is in World 1-2's layout; (2) enemy data - write prgRom 0x20D8 (the enemy list's first byte, 0x0B) -> 0xFF (the end-marker): after reset + re-reach, list_sprites returned only the HUD coin sprite and Mario's 8 entries (count 9, no palette-7 enemy) and the screenshot showed no Goomba at the right edge, while the level itself was identical, proving 0x20D8 is the start of World 1-2's enemy list.

rows.name: per-level timer setting table
rows.notes: The table that sets the TIME each level starts with. It lives at CPU $912D = prgRom 0x112D and is 4 bytes: 20 04 03 02. It is read by the level-start routine in the area-init code at CPU $9182 (LDY $0715 / BEQ skip / LDA $0757 / BEQ skip / LDA $912D,Y / STA $07F8), where Y = $0715, the value unpacked from the layout header's byte 0 bits 6-7 by LoadAreaData. The routine then sets $07F9=0 and $07FA=1, so the initial TIME = table[$0715]*100 + 1 (one tick makes it a round value; e.g. 401 -> 400). Index 0 (value $20) is never selected because a zero $0715 makes the code skip (BEQ). Levels with $0715=1 start at 400 (table[1]=4), $0715=2 at 300 (table[2]=3), $0715=3 at 200 (table[3]=2). World 1-1 and World 1-2 both use $0715=1 (their layout headers' top bits are 01). PROOF (ledgered one-byte write + reset + re-reach + undo): wrote prgRom 0x112E (table[1]) 4 -> 3, reset_emulator, re-entered World 1-2 the usual way; the watch over the level load read $07F8=3, $07F9=0, $07FA=1 then 0, and the paused screenshot showed the HUD reading TIME 300 (vs TIME 400 unedited). undo_edit restored 4.
rows.why: after the ledgered write of 3 at the table's second byte, 1-2 starts at TIME 300 in this screenshot (400 in f79993057c5b.png); the note's bytes 20 04 03 02 at $912D give the hundreds digit per level type

rows.name: area object decoder
rows.notes: Area object decoder: reads a level's layout record stream through the pointer $E7/$E8 (set at level start by LoadAreaData $9C22; World 1-1 -> $A690) and builds the level's objects from it. Body $950A-$9588 (RTS at $9588), with helper subroutines at $9589 and $9595. Per record: $950A saves X, clears $0729, loads Y=$072C (byte offset into the stream) and at $9514 does LDA ($E7),Y / CMP #$FD - $FD ends the data. It then reads the record's second byte ($9520, ASL A: bit7 is a page-break flag that increments the page counter $072A/$072B), re-reads the first byte and masks the low nibble for the object type ($9531-$9537, special types $0D/$0E handled at $9539-$9551; otherwise $9554). When the record's page $072A reaches the target page $0725 it calls the object spawner $9595 ($9565); otherwise it counts a skip ($956B) and advances the data offset with $9589 (INC $072C twice + clear $072B). It loops over the up-to-13 object slots ($9571-$957C: LDA/DEC $0730,X) and returns when $0729 and $0728 are clear. HOW FOUND: trace_writes in read mode over the World 1-1 layout data (CPU $A68E-$A78D) while the attract demo loaded 1-1 returned reads from PCs $9516 (LDA ($E7),Y then CMP #$FD), $9522, $9533 and the spawner's $95A1/$95E9/$95F3/$9600/$962A/$964B, all inside this routine. Disassembling backwards from $9516 past the loop head reached the first instruction $950A (preceded by the RTS at $9503 and six data bytes $10 $51 $88 $C0 $A2 $02 at $9504-$9509). Like other SMB routines it has no direct JSR/JMP (searches for '20 0A 95' and '0A 95' found only incidental bytes), so it is reached by the game's indirect/jump-engine dispatch. PROOF (throwaway hack eval-sheet4-b, ledger seq 1): write_memory prgRom 0x2695 (CPU $A695 = the x byte of the layout record [57 00]) 0x00 -> 0x1F, reset_emulator + reapply_edits, re-entered World 1-1; at the identical camera (TIME 390, same two ? blocks and hill on the left) the normal right-side brick/?-block row was replaced by a totally different built structure (a tall green-capped pipe/wall column), i.e. the decoder read the edited record and built a different object. A control write of $FD over the first layout byte (prgRom 0x2690) removed the interactive pipes/? blocks entirely. undo_edit restored 0x00. Combined with the read trace this proves $950A (reading ($E7),Y at $9514) is the routine that builds the level from the layout records.
